anchors.paper_title: Multi-expert consensus annotations of spontaneous and stimulation-induced seizures in stereotactic EEG
anchors.reason: Title and abstract describe the same multi-expert seizure annotation SEEG dataset (UPenn and CHOP, spontaneous and stimulation-induced seizures) with matching authors, though the preprint counts (83 seizures, 32 patients) differ from the dataset's 78 and 29.
Same title and authors as the dataset (Multi-Expert Seizure Annotation, Ojemann et al.); the Pennsieve Discover record is the original deposit of the same data that NEMAR redistributes.

anchors.paper_title: MNE-BIDS: Organizing electrophysiological data into the BIDS format and facilitating their analysis
anchors.paper_venue: The Journal of Open Source Software
anchors.reason: MNE-BIDS is a software tool for organizing electrophysiology data into BIDS, used in dataset formatting, not a paper describing this seizure annotation dataset.

anchors.paper_title: iEEG-BIDS, extending the Brain Imaging Data Structure specification to human intracranial electrophysiology
anchors.reason: iEEG-BIDS is a specification for organizing intracranial EEG data, which this BIDS-formatted SEEG dataset follows. It does not describe this dataset itself.

metadata.methods_description: Recordings were acquired with a Natus Quantum system at 512-2048 Hz using sEEG depth electrodes (Ad-Tech at HUP; PMT or DIXI Medical at CHOP). Stimulation-induced seizures used bipolar biphasic stimulation. Electrodes were localized by co-registering post-implant CT to pre-implant MRI and parcellating with the Desikan-Killiany atlas in FreeSurfer. Each seizure was annotated independently by multiple epileptologists for unequivocal electrographic onset time and channels.

citation_details.abstract: One-third of the world's 70 million people with epilepsy have seizures that are not controlled by medication; and implantable devices are an exciting option for treatment. These devices improve seizure control and can detect impending attacks, missed medication, and impaired cognition. Unfortunately, they have no way to share this information with their hosts in real-time - a limitation common to most medical devices. This is a missed opportunity for implants and wearables to learn from patients, focus on what matters most to them, and teach them how their behavior affects their health. Here, we present a device platform that converses with patients and learns to co-manage epilepsy. citation_details.title: Unsupervised seizure annotation and detection with neural dynamic divergence
citation_details.author: William K.S. Ojemann, Zhongchuan Xu, Haoer Shi, Katie Walsh, Akash R. Pattnaik, Nishant Sinha, Sarah B. Lavelle, Carlos A. Aguila, Ryan S. Gallagher, Andrew Y. Revell, Joshua J. LaRocque, Jacob Korzun, Catherine V. Kulick‐Soper, Daniel Y Zhou, Peter D. Galer, Saurabh R. Sinha, Russell Taki Shinohara, Kathryn A. Davis, Brian Litt, Erin C. Conrad
citation_details.abstract: Annotating seizure onset and spread in intracranial EEG is essential for epilepsy surgical planning, yet manual annotation is unreliable and cannot scale to large datasets. We introduce Neural Dynamic Divergence (NDD), an unsupervised framework that detects seizure activity by measuring deviation from patient-specific baseline neural dynamics using autoregressive models. NDD requires no labeled training data and adapts to individual patients, channels, and brain states. Validating against expert consensus annotations from 46 seizures, NDD achieves human-level agreement ( ϕ = 0.58 vs. inter-rater ϕ = 0.64) and outperforms existing algorithms on 1,019 seizures with soft labels (AUROC = 0.87). We demonstrate clinical utility by automatically annotating 2,017 seizures, revealing that seizure spread patterns distinguish epilepsy subtypes and predict surgical outcomes. NDD also generalizes to continuous ICU scalp EEG monitoring (AUROC = 0.77). We provide NDD as an open-source Python package

citation_details.abstract: Objective: Cortico-cortical evoked potentials (CCEPs) are used during intracranial EEG (iEEG) monitoring to probe effective connectivity and guide epilepsy surgery. However, the factors governing spatial distribution and variability of stimulation-evoked responses across patients remain incompletely understood, making it difficult to distinguish physiological variation from pathological responses. We aimed to develop interpretable models of CCEP responses that integrate normative and patient-specific features, and to assess how these relationships are influenced by distance, brain-state, and epileptogenicity. Methods: We analyzed single-pulse stimulation data from 34 patients with drug-resistant epilepsy undergoing stereo-EEG monitoring. Significant CCEP responses were defined using N1 peak amplitude. citation_details.title: Cortical stimulation reveals effective disconnection of the epileptogenic network at seizure onset
citation_details.author: Patrick W. Davis, Samuel B. Tomlinson, Caren Armstrong, Erin C. Conrad, William K.S. Ojemann, Jurriaan M. Peters, Brian Litt, Carley A. Gilman, Benjamin C. Kennedy, Eric D. Marsh
citation_details.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Seizure onset, the transition from interictal to ictal network states, remains poorly understood despite decades of research. To date, most analyses of seizure onset rely on descriptors of passively recorded network variables such as spectral features or functional connectivity. However, direct causal analysis of brain network dynamics across the ictal transition have yet to be systematically studied. We therefore sought to characterize the ictal transition using active network probing via corticocortical evoked potentials (CCEPs) generated by direct cortical stimulation. METHODS: We analyzed a unique dataset of pediatric and adult epilepsy patients in whom electroclinical seizures were triggered by low-frequency (<2 Hz) direct cortical stimulation. CCEP amplitudes were quantified preceding, during, and following seizure onset, comparing responses within versus outside the spontaneous seizure onset zone (SOZ) across anatomic locations and seizure onset patterns. citation_details.title: iEEG HFO
citation_details.author: Pennsieve (University of Pennsylvania)
citation_details.abstract: Detects high-frequency oscillations (ripples and fast ripples) on every good channel of intracranial EEG with epycom's line-length, RMS or CS detector and writes the events and rates per channel; recordings sampled below 1000 Hz are skipped by design.

citation_details.title: Seizure Onset Consensus
citation_details.author: Pennsieve (University of Pennsylvania)
citation_details.abstract: Fuses the channel rankings of seizure-onset localisation methods (DynaSD channel recruitment, Epileptogenicity Index, neural fragility) into one seizure-onset-zone estimate per SEEG/ECoG recording, and scores every method and the consensus against expert onset labels (AUC, precision/recall/F1, SzCORE event scoring of the detected onset).

citation_details.title: iEEG Prep
citation_details.author: Pennsieve (University of Pennsylvania)
citation_details.abstract: The first step of the epilepsy iEEG workflows. Reads BIDS-iEEG datasets (MNE-BIDS) or plain EDF, BrainVision, FIF and MEF3 recordings with optional expert labels, keeps the SEEG/ECoG channels, finds bad channels, re-references (bipolar by default), notch- and high-pass-filters, and writes one BIDS-iEEG derivative (EDF+ with per-channel range and sidecars carrying SOZ, resected, onset and spread labels and coordinates) plus a QC table and figures.

citation_details.title: Seizure Neural Fragility
citation_details.author: Pennsieve (University of Pennsylvania)
citation_details.abstract: Computes neural fragility (Li et al. 2021) of each iEEG channel around a seizure onset with the EZFragility R package, in 250 ms windows from 60 s before to 30 s after the onset, and writes the mean fragility before and after onset and the channel ranking, for seizure onset zone localisation in the Seizure Onset Localisation workflow.

citation_details.title: Epileptogenicity Index
citation_details.author: Pennsieve (University of Pennsylvania)
citation_details.abstract: The Epileptogenicity Index of Bartolomei, Chauvel and Wendling (2008) per channel and seizure from intracranial EEG, reimplemented in Python from the paper. A step of the Seizure Onset Localisation workflow.

citation_details.title: Seizure Onset (DynaSD)
citation_details.author: Pennsieve (University of Pennsylvania)
citation_details.abstract: Seizure onset time and per-channel onset, recruitment and score from intracranial EEG, with DynaSD (neural dynamic divergence; by default LiNDDA, a linear forecaster of each recording's pre-ictal dynamics). A step of the Seizure Onset Localisation workflow.

citation_details.title: iEEG Spikes
citation_details.author: Pennsieve (University of Pennsylvania)
citation_details.abstract: Detects interictal epileptiform discharges on every good channel of intracranial EEG with the Janca et al. 2015 (or Barkmeier et al. 2012) detector from epycom and writes the spikes, spike rates per channel and cross-channel spike events, leaving known seizures out.

citation_details.title: iEEG Epilepsy Report
citation_details.author: Pennsieve (University of Pennsylvania)
citation_details.abstract: The last step of both epilepsy iEEG workflows (Interictal Biomarker Mapping; Seizure Onset Localisation). Reads whatever upstream outputs it is given and writes an offline HTML report with channel rankings, channel maps, ROC AUCs against expert labels, seizure onset times, method rankings and agreement, the consensus onset zone, QC, and methods with versions, parameters and citations. Research use only, not for clinical decisions.
